writing.explanation:
Begin with the concrete question: Return the largest rectangle area under the histogram. For the visible input `[2,1,5,6,2,3]`, the stated result is `10`. Before reading code, name the smallest piece of information that must survive from one step to the next. A stack remembers unfinished work in last-in-first-out order; a queue processes work in first-in-first-out order. Say what each stored item still needs. That is the mental model for Largest Histogram Rectangle; it gives you a reason for each update instead of a line of code to memorise.

The core mechanism is this: When height decreases, pop bars whose right boundary is now known and compute their maximal width. Treat it as a claim to test after every operation. Write down the state before the first operation, update it once, and ask which part of the claim is still true. If an item is skipped, inserted, or removed, explain why that action cannot destroy an answer that should be retained. A useful trace has columns for the current input position, the state before the step, the action, and the state afterward. Use the visible sample until the expected result becomes inevitable rather than merely plausible.

Now inspect the Rust sketch, not just its final expression. The supplied Rust sketch is a starting point. Identify what it stores, how one iteration changes it, and whether it already solves the exact task or only demonstrates a related operation. Vec works as a stack; VecDeque supplies efficient operations at both ends. Avoid removing from the front of a Vec in a long loop. Translate the variable names into roles: input, carried state, temporary candidate, and output. Borrow data that only needs reading; copy or move data only when the algorithm actually needs ownership. If the sketch leaves out parsing or edge handling, list those missing steps before calling it a complete solution.

Finally justify the stated bound, O(n) time · O(n) space. Count how often an item, edge, state, or candidate can enter the main operation; do not infer the bound from the number of loop keywords alone. Check empty containers, one item, repeated equal values, and the work left in the structure after the input ends. Predict the result for a smallest legal input and for one case that stresses the invariant. If your prediction disagrees with a hand trace, repair the state definition before changing code.
